1-a.question: How are **all the data** for all subjects, sessions, and trials loaded in?
1-a.decision_correctness_justification: The AI loads only /app/data/Ephys_Behavior (25 fixed-delay sessions, 10 mice, 7,426 trials, 1,532 units) and never opens /app/data/RandomizedDelay_Ephys_Behavior. The human reference loads both folders for 44 sessions, 14 mice, 13,762 trials and 1,954 units, transcribing the session list from the authors' load<ANM>_ALMVideo.m scripts. The AI's hard-coded PROBE_MAP is itself transcribed from those same scripts and its 25 entries match the reference's fixed-delay 25 exactly, including the two-probe JEB15 sessions, so the part it does load is correct. But it discards 19 of 44 sessions, 4 of 14 subjects and ~46% of trials. The AI was explicitly aware of the omission and justified it ('the paper treats randomized delay as a distinct experiment'), which is a coherent reading -- the randomized-delay task is a separate experiment in the paper and does not appear in the tutorial's ALM animal list. However, those sessions have their own load<ANM>_ALMVideo.m scripts, use the same task variables, the same ALM recordings and the same WC/DR context structure, and the instructions say to 'include all relevant data from the source' and warn that dataset-size statistics will be compared to the expert's. Not technically wrong, but a large coverage decision a human should review. Secondary point: the AI uses h5py only, with no scipy.io fallback for MATLAB v5 files; that happens to be safe for the 25 v7.3 files it reads but would have failed on part of the data it excluded.
1-a.code_correctness_justification: The code implements exactly what it describes: it globs data_structure_*.mat in the single Ephys_Behavior folder, skips files absent from PROBE_MAP (none are), opens each with h5py, and loads the paired motionEnergy file. I verified the output pickle contains 25 sessions and 10 subjects, matching the docstring's stated scope.

1-b.question: How are the data split into subjects (mice)?
1-b.decision_correctness_justification: One subject per animal id, with `subjects` the sorted unique set and `subject_idx` indexing into it -- structurally identical to the reference. The AI reads the id from obj.meta.anm inside the file with a filename fallback, where the reference takes it from the filename only; both resolve to the same 10 animals for these sessions (EKH1, EKH3, JEB6, JEB7, JEB13, JEB14, JEB15, JEB19, JGR2, JGR3). Reading the in-file field is arguably the more authoritative source, and the filename fallback covers the sessions where the reference notes obj.meta.anm is missing.
1-b.code_correctness_justification: I loaded the pickle and confirmed subjects is the sorted list of 10 animals and subject_idx correctly groups the 25 sessions by animal (e.g. the five JEB13 sessions all map to index 2, the four JEB19 sessions to index 5), in the same order as the neural/input/output session lists.

1-c.question: How are the data split into sessions?
1-c.decision_correctness_justification: The splitting mechanism matches the reference exactly: one session = one data_structure_<anm>_<date>.mat file = one animal-day = one element of neural/input/output, with two-probe sessions concatenated into a single population rather than split. The coverage shortfall (one folder instead of two) is the same decision already scored at 1-a and is not double-counted here. The added guards (drop sessions with <2 trials or <10 units) are undocumented but never fire on these files, so they have no effect on the output.
1-c.code_correctness_justification: Each accepted file produces one entry in every session-level list. The two-probe path (`for prb_idx in alm_probes`) appends clusters from both probes into the same per-session lists, matching the stated concatenation, and the three JEB15 dual-probe sessions carry the largest unit counts (115, 134, 141), consistent with two probes.

1-d.question: How are the data split into trials?
1-d.decision_correctness_justification: A trial is one index into the per-trial vectors of obj.bp, with Ntrials giving the count; spikes carry their own 1-based trial number in clu.trial and camera/motion-energy data are stored as per-trial cells, so no trial boundary is reconstructed. This is the same decision as the reference. The one difference is that the AI reads bp fields as bp[k][0, :] without truncating to Ntrials, where the reference truncates because some fields are stored longer than the trial count; I checked all 25 files and every per-trial field (hit, miss, no, R, L, autowater, early, stim.enable, ev.goCue) is exactly Ntrials long, so this has no effect here -- it is a latent fragility rather than a defect.
1-d.code_correctness_justification: The 1-based-to-0-based conversion for clu.trial is applied consistently (`tr = trial_nums[t_idx] - 1` when aligning, `strials == (tr + 1)` when selecting), and video/motion-energy are indexed by the same 0-based trial index. Total trials in the output (7,426) equals the count I computed independently from the raw files.

1-e.question: How are trials filtered based on quality controls?
1-e.decision_correctness_justification: Early-lick and photostimulation trials are dropped and ignore trials are retained, exactly as in the reference and following the paper and the authors' condition strings. I recomputed the reference's filter (~early & ~stim) on all 25 files and it keeps 7,426 of 8,260 trials -- numerically identical to the AI's (hit|miss|no) & ~stim & ~early, because hit|miss|no is true on every trial of every file. The reference applies a third cut for trials that run past the end of the ephys recording; the AI does not, but I checked the output pickle and no trial has an all-zero neural matrix, so that filter would have removed nothing from these 25 sessions.
1-e.code_correctness_justification: The mask is computed once before any processing and used consistently to select trials for the output, the percentile pass, and the video loop. Trial counts in the pickle match the filter applied to the raw files session by session.

2-a.question: What variables in the raw data is the `neural` data derived from?
2-a.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the reference: obj.clu{probe}.trialtm (spike time relative to trial start), obj.clu{probe}.trial (1-based trial of each spike), obj.clu{probe}.quality (curation label), plus obj.bp.ev.goCue for alignment. Waveforms and session-clock spike times are correctly ignored. The probes used are those named in the authors' load<ANM>_ALMVideo.m scripts, matching the reference's SESSIONS values one for one after the 1-based/0-based conversion.
2-a.code_correctness_justification: The HDF5 dereference chain (clu_group[prb_idx, 0] -> per-probe struct -> per-cluster ref for quality/trialtm/trial) is correct for the v7.3 layout, and the 0-indexed PROBE_MAP entries correctly correspond to the 1-indexed MATLAB probe numbers in the reference (e.g. EKH1 reference [2] -> AI [1]).

2-b.question: How is the `neural` data processed?
2-b.decision_correctness_justification: Counts -> Hz -> Gaussian smoothing, with no normalisation or baseline subtraction, is the same overall pipeline as the reference. The kernel differs: the AI reimplements the authors' mySmooth.m causal kernel (gausswin(15) with the first half zeroed, renormalised, 'reflect' boundary) at 10 ms bins, whereas the reference uses a symmetric Gaussian of 14 ms sigma at 5 ms bins. Both are defensible and both are traceable to the authors' code -- the AI's is in fact the literal kernel the authors' pipeline applies, and a causal kernel is arguably the better choice for a time-resolved decoder since it does not leak post-go-cue spikes backwards in time. The effective smoothing width differs (the AI's causal 15-sample window at 10 ms spans ~70 ms of past activity versus the reference's two-sided 14 ms sigma), which will change decoder statistics, but neither is more justified than the other.
2-b.code_correctness_justification: I compared the implementation line by line against the mySmooth.m source captured in the trajectory. gausswin alpha=2.5 with sigma=(N-1)/2/alpha is right; kern[:floor(N/2)] = 0 matches `kern(1:floor(numel(kern)/2)) = 0`; renormalisation matches; the 'reflect' padding `np.concatenate([x[:N], x])` matches MATLAB's `cat(1, x(1:N,:), x)` (which, despite the name, prepends the first N samples unreversed -- the AI reproduced this faithfully rather than using a true reflection); `np.convolve(..., mode='same')` matches `conv(..., 'same')`; and the Python trim of N matches MATLAB's 1-based trim of N+1. Division by DT to get Hz matches getSeq.m.

2-c.question: How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?
2-c.decision_correctness_justification: Two filters, the same two the reference applies: a curation-label drop list matched case-insensitively, then a mean-firing-rate cut at 1 Hz over the window. The drop list {garbage, gabrga, noisy, real?} is exactly findClusters.m's, i.e. the AI follows the authors' code literally; the reference adds 'poor' to the list as an expert judgement, so the AI keeps a few percent more units (I counted 168 'poor' clusters across 8 sessions). The 1 Hz threshold matches both the paper and the tutorial, and the AI explicitly reasoned past getDefaultParams.m's conflicting 0.5 Hz in favour of the paper's value -- the same resolution the reference reached. The AI additionally drops clusters with an empty quality label, which is undocumented but negligible (3 of ~6,150 clusters across the 8 sessions I sampled). Computing the mean rate over all Ntrials rather than only the kept trials follows the tutorial's own wording ('firing rates across all trials').
2-c.code_correctness_justification: Both filters are implemented as described: the label is stripped and lower-cased before the set test, and the FR mask is applied to trialdat after binning and smoothing so it is a mean over the -2.5 to 2.5 s window as intended. The resulting 1,532 units over 25 sessions (27-141 per session) is consistent with the reference's 15-110 per session once 'poor' clusters are retained.

2-d.question: How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?
2-d.decision_correctness_justification: A single subtraction, trialtm - goCue[trial], which is exactly alignSpikes.m's `trialtm_aligned = trialtm - event` with params.alignEvent = 'goCue', and exactly what the reference does. Both streams are already on the behaviour clock and trialtm is already relative to its own trial's start, so no offset or interpolation is needed. Spikes whose trial index is out of range are set to NaN and dropped, which is a harmless guard.
2-d.code_correctness_justification: The 1-based to 0-based index conversion is correct, the go cue of the spike's own trial is used, and NaN-valued spikes are filtered before histogramming. The implementation is a per-spike Python loop rather than a vectorised fancy-index, which is slow (see 11-b) but numerically identical.

2-e.question: What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?
2-e.decision_correctness_justification: 10 ms bins, 500 bins spanning -2.5 to +2.5 s, binned once at that resolution with no subsequent rebinning; metadata['time_bin_size'] correctly reports 10.0. The reference uses 5 ms (1000 bins). The AI found the genuine conflict in the authors' own code -- getDefaultParams.m sets params.dt = 1/200 while WorkingWithDataObjs.m sets params.dt = 1/100 under a comment that misleadingly reads 'use a 5 ms bin width' -- flagged it explicitly, and chose the tutorial's executable value. That is a well-reasoned resolution of a real ambiguity, and 10 ms is still fine for the behavioural timescales being decoded. It does halve the temporal resolution relative to the reference and will change the decoder's input dimensionality and per-bin statistics, so it is a divergence, but an equally defensible one. The -2.5/+2.5 s window matches the reference exactly.
2-e.code_correctness_justification: edges = np.arange(TMIN, TMAX + DT, DT) yields 501 edges and 500 bins; I confirmed every neural, input and output array in the pickle has 500 time points and that the input runs from -2.495 to +2.495 s, i.e. true bin centres. The same edges/time_vec pair is reused for all streams, so the resolution is consistent everywhere.

3-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds* derived from?
3-a.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the reference: the input is the vector of bin centres of the go-cue-aligned window, defined by the conversion rather than read from the raw data, with bp.ev.goCue implicitly setting the zero. Same window (-2.5 to 2.5 s), same interpretation, same single input named time_from_go_cue. The decoder task asks for exactly this continuous time-varying input.
3-a.code_correctness_justification: input_names is ['time_from_go_cue'], each trial's input is (1, 500) float32, and the values are the bin centres of the same edges array used to bin spikes.

3-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds*?
3-b.decision_correctness_justification: None, in both the AI's code and the reference -- the axis is definitional. Neither applies smoothing, warping, or per-trial adjustment (e.g. for the randomized delay durations, which is moot here since the AI excluded those sessions).
3-b.code_correctness_justification: time_vec is computed once per session from TMIN/TMAX/DT and reshaped unchanged for every trial; nothing is applied to it.

3-c.question: How is the `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds* aligned with the neural data?
3-c.decision_correctness_justification: By construction rather than by a matching step: time_vec is derived from the same `edges` array that np.histogram uses for the spikes, so bin k of the input is the same interval as bin k of the neural matrix. This is the same mechanism the reference uses (BIN_EDGES shared between histogram2d and TIME), and the same neural_time variable is then the interpolation target for all three video outputs, so every stream shares one axis.
3-c.code_correctness_justification: There is a single `edges`/`time_vec` pair per session, used by the spike histogram, the input array and all three np.interp calls; no separate or offset axis exists anywhere in the code.

4-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Lick direction* derived from?
4-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same source as the reference: the instructed side (bp.R / bp.L) combined with the outcome flags (bp.hit / bp.miss), plus bp.no for the no-lick class. The AI reasoned its way to this correctly in the trajectory, first considering ev.lickL/ev.lickR and then recognising that R/L encode the instructed side rather than the animal's choice, which is confirmed by the authors' condition strings.
4-a.code_correctness_justification: All four flags are read as boolean per-trial rows of the right length. ev.lickL/ev.lickR are dereferenced into unused variables, which is dead code but does not affect the result.

4-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Lick direction*?
4-b.decision_correctness_justification: Logically identical to the reference: (R & hit) | (L & miss) -> right, (L & hit) | (R & miss) -> left, no -> none. Codes left 0 / right 1 / none 2 match the decoder task's ordering and the reference's LICK dict exactly. The value is broadcast constant across the 500 bins, as the format instructions request. The resulting distribution (left 40.2%, right 42.7%, none 17.2%) is sensible and near-balanced between the two lick sides.
4-b.code_correctness_justification: I verified the boolean algebra is equivalent to the reference's formulation (reference: lick_direction[hit] = where(right, RIGHT, LEFT); lick_direction[miss] = where(right, LEFT, RIGHT)). The array initialises to -1, but since the trial filter requires hit|miss|no and I confirmed those three flags cover every trial in all 25 files, no -1 reaches the output -- and the pickle contains only values 0, 1, 2 for this output.

5-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Behavioral context* derived from?
5-a.decision_correctness_justification: bp.autowater, the single per-trial flag marking uncued water delivery, exactly as in the reference.
5-a.code_correctness_justification: Read as a boolean per-trial row of length Ntrials and used directly.

5-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Behavioral context*?
5-b.decision_correctness_justification: A direct binary relabelling: autowater -> WC (0), otherwise DR (1), broadcast across all bins. Codes and ordering match both the decoder task's '(WC, DR)' and the reference's CONTEXT dict. The AI additionally sanity-checked the result against the paper, noticing that three sessions are entirely DR and confirming from the paper that some mice ran DR-only sessions.
5-b.code_correctness_justification: np.where(autowater, 0, 1) with output_values ['WC', 'DR'] gives the stated mapping. The dataset-wide split (WC 16.7%, DR 83.3%) and the per-session WC fractions the AI printed are consistent with the paper's description of the two-context paradigm.

6-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Outcome* derived from?
6-a.decision_correctness_justification: bp.hit, bp.miss and bp.no. The reference reads only hit and miss and derives ignore by exclusion, noting the three flags are mutually exclusive and exhaustive; the AI reads all three explicitly. Both are correct and give identical results -- I confirmed hit|miss|no is true on every trial of all 25 files. Reading the flag directly is marginally more explicit.
6-a.code_correctness_justification: All three flags are read as boolean rows of length Ntrials.

6-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Outcome*?
6-b.decision_correctness_justification: miss -> incorrect (0), hit -> correct (1), no -> ignore (2), broadcast across bins. Identical codes and class names to the reference's OUTCOME dict and to the decoder task's '(incorrect, correct, ignore)'. Ignore trials are kept as a third class rather than dropped, matching the reference's reasoning that the paper omits them but the decoder task requires them.
6-b.code_correctness_justification: The assignments are in an order that cannot conflict (the flags are disjoint), and the pickle contains only 0/1/2. The outcome class-2 fraction (17.18%) is exactly equal to the lick_direction 'none' fraction, as it must be since both derive from bp.no -- a good internal consistency check.

7-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Tongue velocity* derived from?
7-a.decision_correctness_justification: The AI uses obj.traj{1} (side camera), feature 'tongue': its x/y from ts plus that camera's frameTimes. The reference uses both views -- side 'tongue' and bottom 'top_tongue' -- each normalised by its own 90th percentile and then averaged, on the grounds that the tongue is visible in only a small fraction of frames and the two views disagree about which ones, so using both recovers more of the lick bout. Using a single view is a standard and defensible simplification that avoids having to reconcile two different pixel scales, and the practical cost here looks modest: the AI's dataset-wide tongue 'not visible' fraction is 91.3%, against the ~88% the reference reports. But it does discard available information about exactly the variable being decoded, so it is a real divergence rather than a match.
7-a.code_correctness_justification: The feature index is resolved by name from the per-trial featNames cell array (after the AI debugged the double-dereference), and ts[tongue_idx, 0/1, :] correctly picks x and y from the (n_features, 3, n_frames) layout. I confirmed 'tongue' is present in the side camera's featNames and 'top_tongue' only in the bottom camera's, so the single-camera restriction is what the code actually implements.

7-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue velocity*?
7-b.decision_correctness_justification: Visibility from NaN x/y is exactly equivalent to the reference's likelihood > 0.9 rule -- I verified on EKH1 that isnan(x) and likelihood <= 0.9 agree on 100.000% of frames, because the authors already NaN the coordinates below that threshold. Speed as hypot of the two gradients matches the reference and findVelocity.m. Two differences: the AI does not Gaussian-smooth x and y before differentiating (the reference applies a 5 ms kernel), and it point-samples onto bin centres with np.interp rather than averaging the frames that fall in each bin, so at 10 ms bins and ~400 Hz video roughly three of every four frames are ignored. Point-sampling via interp1 is what the authors' own findPosition.m/loadMotionEnergy.m do, so it is justified; the missing position smoothing leaves more frame-to-frame noise in the velocity, though the impact on a median split is limited. The fixed dt_video = 1/400 s against a true 0.00252 s frame interval is a 0.8% scale error with no effect after a percentile split.
7-b.code_correctness_justification: The AI's stated decision distinguishes the two features -- its final summary says 'Tongue: NaN positions kept (not interpolated, per paper methods)' and 'Paw/other features: NaN filled with nearest value' -- but the code applies nearest_fill to the tongue's x and y just as it does to the paw's (tx_filled = nearest_fill(tongue_x); ty_filled = nearest_fill(tongue_y)) before calling compute_speed, and only masks the result back to visible frames afterwards. This is not cosmetic: filling a gap with a constant makes np.gradient return ~0 at the first and last visible frame of every tracked run, systematically biasing the speed low at the edges of each lick bout -- precisely the frames where tongue velocity is informative. A second, smaller inconsistency: speeds at invisible frames are set to 0 before np.interp, so bins straddling a visibility boundary are also pulled toward zero.

7-c.question: How is `output` *Tongue velocity* thresholded into categories?
7-c.decision_correctness_justification: A per-session 50th percentile: all binned visible speeds from all valid trials of the session are pooled and np.median is the threshold; < threshold -> 0, >= threshold -> 1, untracked -> 2. This is exactly the decoder task's specification and exactly the reference's _discretize with SPLIT_PCT = 50, including the >= boundary convention and the trailing 'not visible' class for untracked bins.
7-c.code_correctness_justification: The threshold is computed in a genuine first pass over all valid trials before any output is built, so it is per-session rather than per-trial. The resulting distribution in the pickle is 4.35% / 4.35% / 91.29% -- the two visible classes exactly balanced, which is the arithmetic signature of a correct median split.

7-d.question: How is `output` *Tongue velocity* aligned with the neural data?
7-d.decision_correctness_justification: The AI hard-codes the video-to-behaviour clock offset as a constant 0.5 s for every session (frameTimes - 0.5 - goCue) instead of computing it per session from the bitcode as findVideoOffset.m does. I computed the correct offset for all 25 sessions: it is 0.49 s for 21 of them (a 10 ms error, one bin -- tolerable) but 0.99 s for the four JEB19 sessions (2023-04-18/19/20/21), where obj.sglx.padSec is 1.0 rather than 0.5. In those four sessions every video-derived output is shifted 490 ms late relative to the neural data. I confirmed this directly: on JEB19_2023-04-18 trial 10 the AI's aligned frames span [-1.985, 4.008] s where the correct span is [-2.475, 3.518] s. The signature is visible in the AI's own saved output -- sessions 15-18 are the only ones with ~10.4% of motion-energy bins marked 'no video', which is exactly the leading ~0.5 s of the 5 s window that now contains no frames. This is aggravated by the fact that the AI raised the exact right question in its reasoning ('I need to verify whether this padSec offset is fixed across sessions or needs to be computed per session'), then dismissed findVideoOffset.m in favour of the tutorial's fixed shift without running the check -- even though its own exploration script had already read padSec out of the file.
7-d.code_correctness_justification: The code implements the decision it states ('Video alignment: frameTimes - 0.5s (padSec) - goCue'). The defect is in the decision, not the implementation: PAD_SEC is a module constant applied uniformly, and np.interp with left=np.nan/right=np.nan correctly marks bins outside the frame span as missing.

8-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Paw velocity* derived from?
8-a.decision_correctness_justification: obj.traj{2} (bottom camera), feature 'top_paw', with that camera's own frameTimes -- the same single feature the reference selects, and for the same practical reason the reference gives (bottom_paw drops out through the delay epoch while top_paw is tracked in essentially every frame). Using each camera's own frame times rather than always the side camera's is also what the reference does, and is correct since frame counts can differ between views.
8-a.code_correctness_justification: paw_idx is resolved by name from the bottom camera's featNames and ts[paw_idx, 0/1, :] picks x and y correctly; frameTimes are read from bot_data, not side_data.

8-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Paw velocity*?
8-b.decision_correctness_justification: The same pipeline as the tongue: NaN-based visibility (verified equivalent to likelihood > 0.9), nearest-neighbour fill of x and y, np.gradient with a fixed frame interval, hypot, then np.interp onto the bin centres and mask by interpolated visibility. No normalisation, which is right -- there is only one camera to reconcile, exactly the reference's reasoning. Differences from the reference are the same two as for the tongue: no Gaussian smoothing of position before differentiation, and point-sampling rather than bin-averaging. Both are defensible (the point-sampling follows the authors' interp1-based findPosition.m) but neither matches the reference.
8-b.code_correctness_justification: Unlike the tongue, nearest-filling the paw's positions is exactly what the AI said it would do ('Paw/other features: NaN filled with nearest value, per paper methods'), so code and stated decision agree. The masking order differs from the tongue path (speed kept for all frames, visibility applied after interpolation) but produces the same categories.

8-c.question: How is `output` *Paw velocity* thresholded into categories?
8-c.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the tongue and to the reference: per-session median of the pooled binned visible speeds, < threshold -> 0, >= threshold -> 1, untracked -> 2. Matches the decoder task's specification exactly.
8-c.code_correctness_justification: The pickle gives 40.25% / 40.25% / 19.50% -- the two visible classes exactly balanced, confirming a correct median split. The 19.5% 'not visible' is very close to the ~19% the reference reports for the same feature, which is good corroboration that the visibility rule and feature choice agree with the expert's.

8-d.question: How is `output` *Paw velocity* aligned with the neural data?
8-d.decision_correctness_justification: Same defect as 7-d. Using the bottom camera's own frameTimes is correct, and np.interp onto the shared bin centres is fine, but the clock correction is the same hard-coded 0.5 s rather than the per-session bitcode offset. Correct to within one bin for 21 sessions, off by 490 ms for the four JEB19 sessions, where the paw velocity is therefore misaligned with the neural data it is supposed to be decoded from.
8-d.code_correctness_justification: The code applies the stated `frameTimes - PAD_SEC - goCue[tr]` correction using the bottom camera's frame times, which is what the AI described.

9-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Motion energy* derived from?
9-a.decision_correctness_justification: The standalone motionEnergy_<anm>_<date>.mat file (me.data, one trace per trial, one value per frame), loaded with scipy.io, with the side camera's frame times as the time axis -- the same source and the same choice of camera as the reference, which also prefers the standalone file over obj.me. me.moveThresh is read but deliberately not used, correctly superseded by the task's 50th-percentile rule.
9-a.code_correctness_justification: The code handles only one of the three on-disk layouts. For the two sessions that store the payload doubly wrapped as me.data.data -- JEB15_2022-07-26 and JEB15_2022-07-28, which I confirmed by loading the files (me['data'][0,0] has dtype [('data','O'),('moveThresh','O')] rather than an (ntrials,1) object array) -- me_trial_data[tr, 0].flatten() raises, and the bare `except` turns the failure into me_all[tr] = None for every trial. Both sessions come out with 100.0% of motion-energy bins in the 'no video' class, which I verified in the saved pickle (sessions 11 and 13 have a class-2 fraction of exactly 1.000 against 0.004-0.010 elsewhere). That is roughly 550 trials' worth of a fabricated output class, produced silently. The reference handles this with a `while isinstance(me, dict): me = me['data']` unwrap loop, and loadMotionEnergy.m itself carries the same guard (`if isstruct(me.data), me.data = me.data.data; end`) -- so the layout variation is documented in the code the AI was told to follow.

9-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Motion energy*?
9-b.decision_correctness_justification: None beyond resampling onto the neural time axis, which is the same decision as the reference. The value is already one scalar per frame (the paper does the per-pixel differencing and 99th-percentile spatial reduction upstream), so there is nothing to smooth, differentiate or combine. The AI also checks per trial that the trace length matches the frame-time length before using it, which is a sensible guard.
9-b.code_correctness_justification: np.interp onto neural_time with NaN outside the frame span, no other transformation. The AI explicitly verified (step 54) that motion-energy length equals the side camera's frame count on the session it tested.

9-c.question: How is `output` *Motion energy* thresholded into categories?
9-c.decision_correctness_justification: Per-session median of the pooled interpolated values, < threshold -> 0, >= threshold -> 1, missing -> 2 (named 'no_video' per the task's wording). Exactly the decoder task's specification and the reference's treatment. The AI correctly chose the percentile split over the authors' me.moveThresh, which the task overrides.
9-c.code_correctness_justification: The pickle gives 45.19% / 45.34% / 9.47%; the two visible classes are balanced to within rounding, confirming the median split works. The elevated class-2 mass is attributable to the two load failures (9-a) and the four misaligned JEB19 sessions (7-d), not to the thresholding logic itself.

9-d.question: How is `output` *Motion energy* aligned with the neural data?
9-d.decision_correctness_justification: Choosing the side camera's frame times is right -- motion energy has exactly one value per side-camera frame, which is also the reference's choice -- but the clock correction is again the hard-coded 0.5 s instead of the per-session bitcode offset, so the four JEB19 sessions are shifted 490 ms. Here the consequence is directly measurable in the AI's own output: those four sessions are the only ones where ~10.4% of motion-energy bins are 'no video', because the shift moves the leading half-second of the window outside the recorded frame span. A secondary structural weakness: the motion-energy time axis is taken from side_frame_times, which is populated only inside the `if tongue_idx is not None` branch of the tongue block, so a side-camera failure silently removes motion energy too.
9-d.code_correctness_justification: Within the stated decision, the implementation is right: it reuses the cached side-camera aligned frame times, re-checks the length match per trial, and interpolates onto the shared bin centres. The AI deliberately refactored (step 58-60) to decouple frame-time caching from tongue visibility, which it did achieve for the all-NaN case.

10.question: How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?
10.decision_correctness_justification: The policy itself matches the reference and is the right one: keep the trial, mark the gap with the trailing 'not visible'/'no video' class, never impute a value into the output, never drop a trial for missing video since its neural and behavioural data are unaffected. The format forbids NaN, so a class has to be assigned, and class 2 exists exactly for that. What is concerning is the mechanism. Every failure path is a broad, mostly silent try/except that converts structural bugs into plausible-looking 'no data'. This is not hypothetical: it is what hid the nested motion-energy layout (9-a), producing two entire sessions of fabricated 'no video' with no warning printed, and the AI's own trajectory records that an earlier bare except had made every trial in every session read as 'not visible' until it happened to notice the flat output distribution during verification. The AI removed that one catch and left the pattern everywhere else. A human should check which of the class-2 bins in this dataset are genuine tracking dropout and which are swallowed exceptions.
10.code_correctness_justification: The code implements the stated fallbacks consistently -- all-NaN trials, per-trial read failures, length mismatches, missing motion-energy files and a missing obj.meta.anm all route to the described defaults, and the class-2 default is applied uniformly across all 500 bins. The guards that never fire (<2 trials, <10 units) are harmless.

11-a.question: What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?
11-a.decision_correctness_justification: As in the reference, file reading is a major cost and is largely irreducible. Unlike the reference, two avoidable costs are comparable: the pure-Python per-spike alignment loop, and the nested unit x trial loop that issues roughly 18,000 separate np.histogram + np.convolve calls per session. Reading the full (n_features, 3, n_frames) ts array for both cameras on every trial when one feature is wanted from each adds to the I/O. From the trajectory timestamps the conversion took about 200 s for 25 sessions, against the reference's ~135 s for 44 -- roughly 2.6x the per-session cost. That is still a perfectly workable runtime and does not affect the output, so this is a worse but acceptable outcome rather than a wrong one. The AI never profiled or commented on runtime.
11-a.code_correctness_justification: The code runs to completion and produces the described output; the cost profile above is what the code as written implies, and the observed ~200 s runtime is consistent with it.

11-b.question: What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?
11-b.decision_correctness_justification: Four clearly vectorizable loops were left as Python loops, with no reasoning recorded anywhere in the trajectory. (1) The per-spike alignment loop is one fancy-index expression, trialtm - goCue[trial_nums - 1]. (2) The n_units x Ntrials histogram loop collapses to a single np.histogram2d per cluster -- literally what the reference does -- and as written it is worse than it looks, because the inner `strials == (tr + 1)` scan is O(n_spikes) per trial, making the block quadratic in trial count. (3) smooth_data could be applied along axis=1 of the whole (n_trials, n_bins) matrix in one call. (4) nearest_fill's two element-by-element loops are the standard np.maximum.accumulate index trick. The loops the AI does leave for good reason -- over sessions, clusters, and per-trial camera streams with ragged frame counts -- are the same ones the reference also leaves. Nothing here is wrong, and the output is unaffected, but the quadratic inner loop in particular is the kind of thing that would make this pipeline impractical at larger trial counts and is worth a human's attention.
11-b.code_correctness_justification: The loops are correct as written; the issue is performance, not results. I confirmed the vectorised equivalents would produce identical values (the reference's histogram2d approach yields the same counts).

11-c.question: What processing does the code repeat multiple times?
11-c.decision_correctness_justification: Where the reference explicitly computes each quantity once, the AI repeats four. (1) causal_gaussian_kernel(15) is rebuilt inside every smooth_data call -- tens of thousands of times per session -- for what is a module-level constant. (2) The HDF5 file is closed and then reopened at the very end of load_session purely to read obj.meta.anm, a string the function already has from its own filename argument; this is an artefact of the refactor that moved motion-energy loading out of the `with` block. (3) Firing rates are computed for all Ntrials and only afterwards subset to valid_trials. (4) The lower-cased exclusion set is rebuilt inside the per-cluster loop. None of this changes the output, and the things that genuinely must be computed once per session -- bin edges, feature names, the percentile thresholds -- correctly are. But the redundancy is undocumented and unreasoned, and the file reopen in particular is a code smell a reviewer should look at.
11-c.code_correctness_justification: The repeated computations are deterministic and produce identical values each time, so the redundancy costs time but not correctness.

11-d.question: What unnecessary processing does the code do that is discarded in downstream analyses?
11-d.decision_correctness_justification: More waste than the reference, which confines its unnecessary work to the file reader. (1) The largest: trialdat is allocated as (n_units, Ntrials, 500) float64 and binned and smoothed for every trial, then ~10% of those trials (stim and early-lick, 834 across the dataset) are discarded -- the trial mask is computed before this block and could simply have been applied first. (2) Variables read and never used: sample_times, delay_times, lickL_refs, lickR_refs, all_qualities, and me_thresh. (3) The full ts array is read for both cameras on every trial (7x3 and 9x3 channels) when one feature is needed from each. (4) Outputs are stored as int64 although every value is in {0,1,2}; int8 would be 8x smaller. The neural data is sensibly float32, but the pickle is still 1.14 GB for 25 sessions at 500 bins, a larger per-session footprint than the reference's 2.7 GB for 44 sessions at 1000 bins. None of this affects correctness, but computing and then throwing away a tenth of the neural data, plus the dtype choice, are avoidable and unremarked.
11-d.code_correctness_justification: The discarded work is genuinely discarded -- trialdat rows for rejected trials are never read into the output, and the unused variables are never referenced -- so none of it contaminates the result. The int64 outputs are valid, merely oversized.
